Chapter 8: Reclaiming Identity and Personal Power
Abuse has this way of blurring the lines that make us, well, us. Over time, it can feel like your sense of self starts to fade, replaced by someone else’s expectations, demands, or constant criticism.
But here’s the thing—reclaiming your identity is one of the most powerful, and honestly, freeing parts of the healing journey.
Let me share an example. There was a man who’d spent years in a relationship where his interests were always mocked or dismissed. After it ended, he found himself not even sure what he actually liked anymore. Did he really enjoy hiking, or was that just his partner’s thing? Was he someone who loved quiet nights at home, or had he simply learned to keep the peace? Those questions felt huge at first… but they were the start of something new.
Most of us don’t realize just how much our identity can be shaped by other people—especially after abuse. Rediscovering who you are can feel exciting, but it’s also a little scary. It means trying out new things, messing up sometimes, and learning to trust your own instincts again.
Take another story—a woman who grew up in a family that always told her she was “too much.” Too loud, too emotional, too ambitious. When she finally stepped away, she decided to embrace all those parts of herself she’d been taught to shrink. She signed up for improv classes, laughed at her own jokes, and filled her life with people who celebrated her energy. For the very first time, she felt like she was truly seen—and accepted—just as she was.
Reclaiming your personal power often means setting new goals and taking a few risks. For some, it’s going back to school, starting a new job, or moving to a different city. For others, it’s speaking up at work, diving into a creative project, or simply making decisions without waiting for someone else’s approval.
There’s real vulnerability in stepping into the unknown, especially after years of being told you’ll just mess it up. But every little victory—no matter how small—builds your confidence. One person put it perfectly: she said the thrill wasn’t in getting everything right, but in making her own choices, even when things didn’t work out. “At least they were my choices,” she said. “That’s what matters.”
The journey to reclaim your identity is ongoing. There’ll be setbacks, and moments where you doubt yourself. But with time, those old labels—broken, weak, unlovable—start to fade away. And in their place, new words show up: resilient, courageous, worthy.
